facts.text: Gabapentin is contraindicated in patients who have demonstrated hypersensitivity to gabapentin or any of its ingredients.

Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS)/multiorgan hypersensitivity may be fatal or life‑threatening; discontinue gabapentin if signs such as fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, or organ involvement are present and an alternative etiology cannot be established.
Anaphylaxis and angioedema can occur after the first dose or at any time; patients should stop gabapentin immediately and seek emergency medical care.

Gabapentin may impair driving, operating heavy machinery, and cause somnolence, sedation, or dizziness; patients should not drive or use complex machinery until they have sufficient experience to assess their ability.
Abrupt discontinuation of gabapentin can increase seizure frequency or precipitate status epilepticus; taper the drug rather than stopping suddenly.
Antiepileptic drugs, including gabapentin, increase the risk of suicidal thoughts or behavior; monitor patients for depression, suicidal ideation, or mood changes.

Serious or fatal respiratory depression has been reported when gabapentin is used with CNS depressants (e.g., opioids) or in patients with underlying respiratory impairment; monitor closely and consider initiating at a low dose.
facts.population: Patients receiving CNS depressants or with respiratory disease

facts.text: Neuropsychiatric adverse reactions have been observed in children 3–12 years old (emotional lability, hostility, thought disorder, hyperkinesia); monitor pediatric patients for these effects.
Preclinical studies showed increased pancreatic acinar cell tumors in rats; clinical significance in humans is unknown.
Sudden and unexplained deaths have been reported in epilepsy patients treated with gabapentin; incidence is within the range reported for epilepsy populations not receiving gabapentin.
Concomitant use of gabapentin with morphine or other opioids may increase gabapentin plasma concentrations, potentially requiring dose adjustment.
Co‑administration with other central nervous system depressants (e.g., benzodiazepines, barbiturates) can potentiate CNS depression, somnolence, and respiratory depression.
